result.area_summary: The core-infra slice is in strong shape where the repo has clearly invested: the LRU+TTL cache's store-after-invalidate guard (IndexWatch refcounting, hold-across-store, stamp-based rollback) is correct and exhaustively tested; the four-bucket lock split, the {tenant}| key convention, the sign-out sweep across every CacheKind, and the typed-accessor "wrong door misses, never evicts" rule all hold; retry budget, Retry-After honouring, RetryClass and the http_error_enum! taxonomy are single-sourced and pinned by conformance tests; TokenError codes survive every client's BearerProvider boundary. The weak spots are around the edges the invariants do not reach: the documented auto-update opt-out (settings.auto_update / AZAPPTOOLKIT_AUTO_UPDATE) is never read by anything, the Exchange transport still open-codes its retry loop and so replays New-* cmdlets after transient failures (the exact hazard RetryClass was introduced for, invisible to the trust.rs invariant), UserSettings::mutate will overwrite an unparseable settings.json with defaults, and private_file's predictable, symlink-following temp path is used for operator-chosen export locations. Several docs-in-code comments have drifted from the code (per-object cap coverage, "four unified clients", writer count in AGENTS.md).

findings.title: The documented auto-update opt-out (settings.auto_update / AZAPPTOOLKIT_AUTO_UPDATE) is never consulted; UserSettings::load has no production caller
findings.rationale: The whole `auto_update` field, `default_true`, `auto_update_env_override`, and `UserSettings::load` are dead code: nothing in the backend or frontend reads them, so `check_for_update` always egresses to the GitHub release endpoint on launch. README and DEVELOPMENT.md tell MDM/CI operators the opt-out works, and DEVELOPMENT.md refers to a "settings toggle" that does not exist in web-rs either (no `auto_update` binding or view). An operator who set the env var per the docs believes update checks are disabled; they are not — a misleading-the-operator result plus unexpected network egress in locked-down deployments.
findings.proposal: In `check_for_update` (or a thin `update_policy` read before it), load `UserSettings::load(&crate::config_directory())` and return `Ok(None)` when `auto_update == false` for the *launch* path (keep the manual nav button working, or pass an `explicit: bool` arg so a manual check bypasses the policy). Add a unit test on the core side that `load` honours the env var end-to-end and a repo-invariant or GUI test that the launch check is gated. Either implement the "settings toggle" DEVELOPMENT.md mentions or delete that clause. Expected effect: the documented opt-out actually stops the launch-time check.

findings.title: Exchange transport replays non-idempotent cmdlets (New-ManagementRoleAssignment, New-ServicePrincipal, New-ManagementScope) after transient failures — the open-coded loop has no RetryClass and escapes the trust.rs invariant
findings.rationale: Every Exchange admin call is a POST to InvokeCommand, and `send_core` retries a connection reset or 5xx up to MAX_RETRIES times regardless of the cmdlet. A `New-ManagementRoleAssignment` that committed server-side before a 502 is re-run and creates a second, identical role assignment; a later `Remove-ManagementRoleAssignment` by identity removes one and the app keeps its mailbox access — the operator sees "removed" while access persists. `New-ServicePrincipal`/`New-ManagementScope` replays surface as "already exists" failures after a successful write. This is exactly the class `RetryClass::NonIdempotent` closed for Graph/ARM/Key Vault, but the `trust.rs` invariant scans only `with_retries(` call sites, so the hand-rolled Exchange loop is invisible to it. http_retry.rs's own header ("Shared retry policy for the Graph, ARM, Key Vault and Exchange HTTP clients") and the `with_retries` doc ("The four HTTP clients each open-coded this loop", past tense) both state a unification that has not happened for Exchange.
findings.proposal: Port `send_core` onto `with_retries(label, class, |_| ...)`, deriving `class` from the cmdlet verb: `Get-`/`Test-`/`Search-` → Idempotent; `New-`/`Add-`/`Remove-`/`Set-`/`Update-` → NonIdempotent (Set-/Remove- are semantically idempotent on Exchange but a replay after an unknown outcome still risks double side effects; be conservative, as the Graph path is). Keep the diagnostics-header capture inside the per-attempt closure. Extend `repo_invariants/trust.rs` to also fail on any crate source (outside http_retry.rs) that references `MAX_RETRIES` or `next_backoff_ms` directly, so a future hand-rolled loop cannot reappear. Update the http_retry.rs header/with_retries docs to match.

findings.title: UserSettings::mutate overwrites an unparseable or unreadable settings.json with defaults — vault bindings and tenant defaults are permanently lost
findings.rationale: The atomic temp-and-rename closed the *torn write* cause of an unparseable file, but `mutate` still treats "file exists but cannot be parsed" and "file exists but cannot be read (EACCES, EIO, AV lock on Windows)" identically to "file missing", then serialises defaults over it. Any of: a hand-edit typo (which defaults.rs explicitly expects), a future field type change, or a transient read failure, followed by the very next `mutate` (sign-in calls `remember_account` via `mutate` on every successful login) wipes `tenant_defaults` including `app_vaults` — the map the rotation flow needs to find secrets again — and the only trace is a `warn!` in the log. Data loss with no recovery.
findings.proposal: Make `from_file` return `Result<Option<Self>, io::Error>` distinguishing `ErrorKind::NotFound` (→ `Ok(None)`) from parse/IO failures. Keep `stored()`'s lenient fallback for read-only callers, but have `mutate` refuse (`Err(InvalidData)`) when the file exists and cannot be parsed — or first rename it to `settings.json.corrupt-<timestamp>` and log at `error!` before writing defaults. Callers already treat `mutate` errors as non-fatal (state.rs:347-355, keyvault.rs:167-171). Add a test: write `not json`, call `mutate`, assert the original bytes (or a `.corrupt` sibling) survive.

findings.title: private_file::write_then_rename uses a predictable, symlink-following temp path — exploitable in operator-chosen (possibly shared) export directories
findings.rationale: The temp name is `<target>.tmp<pid>` — pid is readable by any local user — and the open is `create(true)` without `create_new`/`O_NOFOLLOW`, deliberately reusing a pre-existing temp. In a shared or world-writable export directory (the operator picks the path via a save dialog; `/tmp` or a shared drive is plausible) another local user can pre-plant `<name>.tmp<pid>` as a symlink to a file the victim owns. The write then truncates and overwrites that victim-owned file with the secret payload (fchmod on the fd succeeds because the victim owns the target), and `rename(temp, path)` moves the symlink itself into place. Result: destruction of an arbitrary victim-owned file and the secret landing where the attacker chose. The app-config directory is per-user so `settings.json` is not exposed, but the export choke point is.
findings.proposal: Open the temp with `.create_new(true)` (O_EXCL) and, on unix, `.custom_flags(libc::O_NOFOLLOW)` — or, without libc, rely on `create_new` which refuses to follow an existing symlink. Add a short random/monotonic component to the temp name (e.g. `.tmp{pid}-{counter}` from an `AtomicU64`, or `SystemTime` nanos) and retry once on `AlreadyExists`. This removes the need to `set_permissions` on a reused temp; keep it for belt-and-braces. Optionally `File::open(parent)?.sync_all()` after the rename on unix so the rename is durable across a crash. Add a test that a pre-existing temp symlink causes the write to fail rather than follow.

findings.title: UserSettings::save is a public, unlocked writer duplicating save_locked, with a doc block that contradicts the module's own invariant
findings.rationale: The module states that `save_locked` is private precisely so nobody can split read-modify-write apart, yet `save` — the same body, public, unlocked — remains as the open door for the next writer; the "only writer of this file" / "first-run config screen" doc is stale (config.rs uses `mutate`) and has been spliced onto `mutate`'s doc. No repo invariant pins "settings writers go through mutate".
findings.proposal: Delete `save` (convert the two tests that call it to `mutate`, or make it `#[cfg(test)]`), have `save_locked` be the only serialiser, and split the doc block so `mutate` carries only its own text (move the owner-only rationale to `save_locked`). Optionally add a `repo_invariants` scan that `UserSettings::stored(` is never followed by a write in the same function.

findings.title: http_error/http_retry docs claim all four clients are unified; Exchange still has a hand-written enum and loop, and the macro doc miscounts its variants
findings.rationale: The macro cannot express Exchange's `Forbidden { detail, had_diagnostics }` (it only supports *extra* variants, not a replacement shape), so Exchange being outside the macro is a legitimate consequence — but the docs present the unification as complete, and the miscount suggests the doc was not re-read after `Protocol` was added. A reader trusting the header would not look for a fourth `ui_code` table to keep in sync.
findings.proposal: Either (a) add an optional `forbidden = { $($field:ident : $ty:ty),* }` override arm to `http_error_enum!` so `ExchangeError` can join, keeping one `ui_code` table for all four; or (b) correct both module docs to say three clients share the macro and name Exchange's `had_diagnostics` Forbidden as the reason it stays hand-written, and fix "nine" → "ten". (a) is the durable fix and pairs naturally with the Exchange retry-loop port.

findings.title: Docs-in-code drift around the cache caps and the settings writer count
findings.rationale: Each of these was true once and drifted when `Lists` joined the per-object cap and when `mutate` replaced `stored`+`save`. AGENTS.md is read by every agent on session start, so its stale writer count and wrong function name actively misdirect the next change to settings.json.
findings.proposal: Update constants.rs:58-61 to name both kinds and reference `Cache::cap_for`; change cache.rs:4-5 and constants.rs:47-48 to say the cap is `MAX_CACHE_SIZE` for aggregate kinds and `MAX_PER_OBJECT_CACHE_SIZE` for `ServicePrincipal`/`Lists`; change AGENTS.md:110 to "four writers read-modify-write via `UserSettings::mutate`".

findings.title: TenantDefaults has three copy-pasted pattern resolvers, each carrying the same 8-line comment (including Exchange-scope text on the Key Vault resolver)
findings.rationale: Three copies of a load-bearing guard (the placeholder check that prevents every app collapsing onto one scope/group/secret name) are three places a future edit can miss; the commands layer (`commands/defaults.rs:53-57`) already iterates the three patterns as a table, so the core side should too. The duplicated comment also misattributes the Exchange rationale to the secret-name resolver.
findings.proposal: Add `fn resolve_pattern(pattern: Option<&str>, default_prefix: &str, app_id: &str) -> String` holding the guard and the comment once; make the three public methods one-liners over it. Keep the existing tests (they exercise all three), and add one asserting `resolve_pattern` directly. Optionally rename `SCOPE_NAME_PLACEHOLDER` → `NAME_PATTERN_PLACEHOLDER` since it now serves three patterns.

findings.title: No cache test covers clear()/clear_kind() racing an in-flight IndexWatch (the diagnostics "Clear cache" path)
findings.rationale: The `bump_watches` calls in `clear`/`clear_kind` are the only thing stopping an operator's "Clear cache" click mid-scan from being followed by a re-pinned pre-clear index for the full TTL — and `clear_kind(Audit)` must *not* refuse a concurrent `Lists` index store. Neither direction is asserted, and both are one-line regressions away (drop a `bump_watches`, or pass `None` instead of `Some(kind)`).
findings.proposal: Add two tests beside the existing watch tests: (1) `generation_for(Lists, k)` → `clear()` → `put_typed_index_if_current` returns false and the key stays empty; (2) `generation_for(Lists, k)` → `clear_kind(Audit)` → store succeeds. Both are ~10 lines using the existing helpers.

findings.title: CacheKind::idx is `self as usize` while the bucket array is sized by the hand-maintained ALL — a new variant compiles and panics with index-out-of-bounds on first use
findings.rationale: The comment's claim is only half true: `ttl_for`'s exhaustive match forces a TTL arm, but a developer who adds `CacheKind::Foo`, a `ttl_for` arm and `record`/`CacheStats` arms gets a clean compile and a runtime panic (`index out of bounds: the len is 4 but the index is 4`) the first time `Foo` is read or written — inside a Tauri command, taking the request down. Nothing ties `ALL.len()` to the variant count.
findings.proposal: Make `idx()` an exhaustive `match self { ServicePrincipal => 0, Permissions => 1, Audit => 2, Lists => 3 }` (so a new variant is a compile error here too) and add `const _: () = assert!(CacheKind::ALL.len() == CacheKind::Lists as usize + 1);` plus a unit test `for (i, k) in ALL.iter().enumerate() { assert_eq!(k.idx(), i) }`. Alternatively collapse `CacheStats`'s eight fields and `record` into `[Counters; ALL.len()]` indexed by `idx()`, removing two more hand-maintained tables.

findings.title: mutate's process-wide lock does not cover a second app instance; std's File::lock (stable since 1.89, MSRV 1.98) would close the gap without a dependency
findings.rationale: The lost-update race `mutate` fixes reappears across processes: two windows/instances (nothing prevents launching a second) each read-modify-write settings.json; the atomic rename means the file is never torn, but the second writer's snapshot silently drops the first's field (e.g. a vault binding recorded by a rotation in one instance is overwritten by a defaults save in the other). Since MSRV is 1.98, `std::fs::File::lock`/`try_lock` (stabilised in 1.89) gives a cross-process advisory lock with no new crate.
findings.proposal: In `mutate`, after taking `SETTINGS_LOCK`, open (create) `<config_dir>/settings.lock` and call `.lock()?` on it for the duration of the read-modify-write; the guard drops with the `File`. This composes with the atomic rename and keeps `stored()` lock-free for readers. Alternatively adopt `tauri-plugin-single-instance`, but that is a dependency and a broader behaviour change.

minor_nits: crates/azapptoolkit-core/src/cache.rs:1046-1051 — the doc comment for `release_watch` ("Drops one reference to a watch...") sits directly above `peek_watch`, which then has its own one-line doc; the two blocks are merged and `release_watch` (line 1058) is undocumented.

crates/azapptoolkit-core/src/cache.rs:793-800 — `store_if_current` returns `true` when `store` returned `None` (caching disabled / serialize failure) although the doc says it returns `false` when the store was skipped; return `stamp.is_some()` on the success arm (callers currently ignore the bool).

crates/azapptoolkit-core/src/cache.rs:697 — the poisoned-entry eviction in `get` uses `remove(key)` after the bucket lock was dropped in `lookup`, so it can evict an entry a concurrent writer just replaced; `lookup` could hand back the stamp and use the existing `remove_if_stamp` for consistency with `store_if_current`.

crates/azapptoolkit-core/src/cache.rs:189 — `Bucket::touch` allocates `key.to_string()` on every cache hit under the bucket lock; storing LRU keys as `Arc<str>` (shared with `entries`) would make the hot-path row a refcount clone.

crates/azapptoolkit-core/src/http_retry.rs:61-72 — `parse_retry_after_seconds(Some("0"))` → `retry_after_millis(0)` = 0 ms, so a `Retry-After: 0` yields MAX_RETRIES back-to-back attempts with no backoff or jitter; consider flooring the explicit header at e.g. 500 ms.

crates/azapptoolkit-core/src/token.rs:63-73 — `From<String>` and `From<&str>` for `TokenError` have no users (every site uses `TokenError::new`/`opaque` explicitly) and exist only to let a `?`/`.into()` silently flatten to `token_error`, the anti-pattern the type's doc warns about; remove them.

crates/azapptoolkit-core/src/cache/tests.rs:53 and crates/azapptoolkit-core/src/defaults.rs:217 — `use super::*;` appears mid-module after tests that already rely on it; move to the top of each test module.

crates/azapptoolkit-core/src/settings.rs:404-429 and crates/azapptoolkit-core/src/private_file.rs:95-112 — two identical hand-rolled `TempDir` helpers (the no-`tempfile` decision is documented); a `#[cfg(test)] pub(crate) mod test_support` would hold one copy.
crates/azapptoolkit-core/src/cache.rs:42 — comment "matches enum declaration order" is the only thing tying `ALL` to `idx()`; see the CacheKind::idx finding.
docs/DEVELOPMENT.md:314 — refers to "the settings toggle" for auto-update; no such toggle exists in web-rs (no `auto_update` binding or view).
result.coverage_notes: All files in the slice were read end to end: cache.rs (1124 lines), cache/tests.rs (1102), http_retry.rs, http_error.rs, settings.rs, private_file.rs, token.rs, net.rs, defaults.rs, constants.rs, lib.rs, Cargo.toml, plus reauth.rs and redirect.rs for cross-references. Outside the slice I read only the portions needed to verify claims: exchange/src/client/transport.rs (1-290), exchange/src/error.rs (1-140), exchange rbac.rs/groups.rs mutating call sites, graph batch.rs (40-60, 220-275), graph/keyvault/arm bearer-mapping lines, service_principals.rs (270-365), commands/applications/cache.rs (60-135, 186-226), commands/{defaults,config,keyvault,updater,diagnostics,search,export,credentials}.rs excerpts, state.rs (225-240, 340-380), web-rs shell.rs (152-200), repo_invariants/cache.rs (test names only) and trust.rs (140-200), arm error.rs + error_conformance.rs heads. I did not read repo_invariants/cache.rs bodies in full, the remaining Exchange client files, or web-rs beyond shell.rs/bindings/updater.rs. No cargo build/test/clippy was run per instructions; conclusions about dead code (`UserSettings::load`, `auto_update`, the `TokenError` From impls) rest on repo-wide grep, not on compiler dead-code diagnostics.

result.area_summary: The core audit module is in strong shape: every rule is a focused helper folded in order, scope-awareness consistently carries the resource (ResourcePermission) and gates positively, (resource, value) dedup and the redundancy planner are order-independent and well pinned, and two characterization snapshots plus ~60 rule tests cover most branches. The weak spots are risk-model consistency rather than mechanics: Rule 13 flags declared delegated scopes while its own docs and the UI group promise admin-consented ones; the risk tables apply their stated write=high / read=medium rule unevenly (Calendars.ReadWrite medium, Contacts.Read / MailboxSettings.Read / Device.Read.All zero); Rule 7 counts multi-year certificates as "long-lived secrets" while Rule 17 pushes toward certificates; and three emitted issue markers have no finding group, so org-wide reach on the legacy Office 365 resources is scored but invisible in the findings-first workbench. Several in-code docs have drifted from the code after the recent resource-aware refactors, and the legacy PowerShell citations the module rests on are unverifiable from the repo.

findings.title: Rule 13 flags declared delegated scopes regardless of consent, while its predicate doc and the UI group promise admin-consented ones
findings.rationale: For an app-registration row `scope_values` is the manifest's declared delegated scopes, and `rule_high_risk_delegated` never consults `perms.has_admin_consent`. Since the rule was widened to the broad-prefix predicate (`Mail.`, `Files.`, `Group.`, `Sites.`, `Directory.`…), every app that merely declares a user-consent `Mail.Read` or `Files.Read` delegated scope now lands in the "High-risk delegated permissions" group whose blurb says "Admin-consented delegated scopes". Delegated access under user consent is confined to the consenting user, so the group misleads the operator and buries the genuinely admin-consented cases. The only Rule 13 test (tests.rs:394-415) exercises just the two exact entries plus `User.Read`, so the broad-prefix behaviour under `score_application` is unpinned.
findings.proposal: Keep the two exact PS-ported entries (`Directory.AccessAsUser.All`, `user_impersonation`) unconditional, but apply the broad-prefix half only when `perms.has_admin_consent` is true (or, better, thread the per-client AllPrincipals scope set the runner already keeps for SP rows so consent is decided per scope). Add table rows: declared `Mail.Read` without admin consent → no issue; declared `Mail.Read` + `has_admin_consent` → issue. Update the rule doc to say which half is consent-gated.

findings.title: `Calendars.ReadWrite` sits in the medium table, contradicting the tables' own "tenant-wide WRITE is high" rule
findings.rationale: The file states the weighting rule explicitly and applies it to Mail, Contacts, MailboxSettings, Chat, Device, Notes and Files — but `Calendars.ReadWrite` (write to every calendar in every mailbox, its own comment says) stays at 5 points while `Contacts.ReadWrite` earns 10. An app with org-wide calendar write ranks Low (5 < RISK_MEDIUM=8) while the same reach on contacts ranks Medium. No test guards the write-half placement; `mailbox_family_risk_entries_agree_with_the_scoping_role_map` only checks spelling.
findings.proposal: Move `Calendars.ReadWrite` to `HIGH_RISK_APP_PERMISSIONS` (+ CHANGELOG entry, since it shifts ranking per AGENTS.md). Add a test asserting every mailbox-family value ending in `ReadWrite` that `graph_mail_role` maps is in the HIGH table, so a future family addition cannot land in the wrong tier silently.

findings.title: Read halves of several high-weighted families score zero (Contacts.Read, MailboxSettings.Read, Device.Read.All, Notes.Read.All, Application.Read.All)
findings.evidence:
permissions.rs SUBSUMED table (narrower side only, none in either risk table):
313:    ("MailboxSettings.Read", &["MailboxSettings.ReadWrite"]),
319:    ("Contacts.Read", &["Contacts.ReadWrite"]),
375:        "Device.Read.All",
383:        "Application.Read.All",
405:    ("Notes.Read.All", &["Notes.ReadWrite.All"]),

MEDIUM table (lines 132-157) contains `Mail.Read`, `Files.Read.All`, `Sites.Read.All`, `Chat.Read.All`, `Calendars.Read` — but not the five above.

permissions.rs:672-676 (test scope):
    /// scans table -> role map ... It cannot catch an entry that was never written
    fn every_broader_subsuming_permission_carries_a_risk_weight()  — walks only `broaders`.
findings.rationale: `Contacts.Read` is a Graph mailbox-family permission `graph_mail_role` maps (scoping.rs:88), so Rule 11 raises "Organization-wide mailbox access: Contacts.Read" for it — yet it contributes 0 points while `Calendars.Read` (same family, same reach class) contributes 5. `MailboxSettings.Read` reads every mailbox's forwarding/auto-reply settings; `Device.Read.All` and `Application.Read.All` are tenant-wide directory reads on par with `Group.Read.All` (medium). The existing guard test deliberately checks only the broader side of the subsumption table, so these narrower-side omissions are invisible.
findings.proposal: Add `Contacts.Read`, `MailboxSettings.Read`, `Device.Read.All`, `Notes.Read.All` (and decide on `Application.Read.All`) to `MEDIUM_RISK_APP_PERMISSIONS`, with a CHANGELOG note. Extend the guard test with a narrower-side walk for the mailbox family: every value `graph_mail_role` maps must be in HIGH or MEDIUM, or be listed in an `INTENTIONALLY_UNSCORED` table with a reason (`Mail.ReadBasic*` would be the documented exceptions).

findings.title: Rule 7 counts multi-year certificates as "long-lived secrets", penalizing the migration Rule 17 recommends
findings.rationale: `all_creds` chains secrets and certificates, so a standard 2-year PKI certificate scores +3 under an issue literally titled "Long-lived secrets". Rule 17 tells the operator to replace secrets with certificates; doing so with a normal certificate lifetime raises the app's score and files a misnamed finding. The constant is documented as `LONG_LIVED_SECRET_DAYS` (Credential-Analysis.ps1:169) — a secret threshold. The only certificate test (`certificates_do_not_trip_long_lived_when_no_dates`, tests.rs:1933) covers the no-dates case; nothing pins that a dated long-lived certificate is flagged, so narrowing the rule breaks no test.
findings.proposal: Restrict `is_long_lived` to `CredentialKind::Secret` (or add a separate, longer certificate threshold, e.g. >3 years, worded "Long-lived certificate"). Add table rows: 400-day secret → +3; 400-day certificate → 0 (or the cert tier). CHANGELOG note since it shifts ranking.

findings.title: Three emitted issue markers have no finding group or posture count, so unconfinable org-wide reach is scored but invisible in the workbench
findings.evidence:
types.rs:558-563 (module doc of `issue`):
/// Stable markers the UI keys audit facets/home cards off. The scorer emits
/// issues that **start with** these ... the frontend matches the same constants ...
types.rs:576, 588, 606: UNSCOPABLE_LEGACY_MAILBOX / UNCONFINABLE_MAILBOX / UNCONFINABLE_SHAREPOINT

apps/desktop/web-rs/src/views/audit_view/filter.rs:61-95 `issue_marker` keys: high_risk_perms, high_risk_delegated, external_exposure, orgwide_mailbox, scoped_mailbox, legacy_mailbox_scope, orgwide_sharepoint, redundant_perms, scoped_sites, ownership — none for the three above.
apps/desktop/web-rs/src/views/audit_view/groups.rs:47-136 GROUP_CATALOG: same key set.
Only consumer: row.rs:65-66 (tab routing).
findings.rationale: An app holding `Contacts.Read` on Office 365 Exchange Online (score 0, `is_unscopable_legacy_exchange_permission` true) or `Sites.Manage.All` on Office 365 SharePoint Online (score 0) gets a scorer finding that reaches every mailbox/site, yet appears in no findings group, no posture count and no filter — it is only discoverable by reading the issues column in the All-apps pane or the export. The scorer deliberately keeps these out of `orgwide_mailbox`/`orgwide_sharepoint` so they carry no Fix, which is correct, but the workbench then has no advisory home for them. This is the same shape as `high_risk_perms` (Actionable, no bulk fix).
findings.proposal: Add an advisory group (e.g. key `unconfinable_reach`, title "Org-wide reach the toolkit cannot confine") in `GROUP_CATALOG` + `issue_marker`, matching the three markers with `starts_with`, no remediation kinds, tab "permissions"; count it in `posture_counts`. On the core side, add the three markers to `emitted_issue_markers_are_stable` so the doc claim "asserts the scorer still emits each" becomes true.

findings.title: Bare-value `least_privilege_alternative` assumes Graph, and the permission picker calls it while holding the resource id
findings.rationale: The picker is the "full live catalog (every resource)" per the architecture doc, so an operator selecting the Office 365 Exchange Online `Mail.Read` appRole sees "Org-wide — tenant-wide reach. Scope to specific mailboxes (Exchange RBAC)." — advice the toolkit's own `is_scopable_exchange_resource_permission` says cannot be applied on that resource. AGENTS.md says the value-only scopable forms are pinned out; this Graph-defaulting wrapper is the one remaining value-only entry point, and its sole caller has the resource in scope two lines above.
findings.proposal: Remove `least_privilege_alternative` from `mod.rs` re-exports (or mark `#[deprecated]`), change `scope_hint(resource_app_id: &str, value: &str)` to call `least_privilege_alternative_for(Some(resource), value)`, and add the bare-value name to the repo_invariants source scan that pins the other deleted value-only helpers.

findings.title: Redundant narrower permissions still carry their own weight, so identical effective access scores differently
findings.rationale: `deduped()` exists because scoring a duplicate grant twice let identical effective access rank differently. A fully-covered narrower Graph permission is the same situation one step removed: `Mail.ReadWrite`+`Mail.Read` (15, High) has exactly the reach of `Mail.ReadWrite` alone (10, Medium), and `Directory.ReadWrite.All` + `User.Read.All` + `Group.Read.All` scores 20 vs 10. Rule 18 already computes the covered set. This is a risk-model judgment (surface area vs. reach), but today it is neither scored-as-reach nor documented as intentional.
findings.proposal: Either (a) exclude grants that `redundant_app_permissions` reports as covered from the Rule 1&2 tally (score = effective reach; the redundancy finding + Fix still surface the surplus), with a CHANGELOG note and updated snapshots; or (b) add one sentence to audit-findings-and-remediation.md's Rule 18 section stating that redundant grants keep their weight on purpose. Pick and pin with a test either way.

findings.title: `deduped()` clones the `mail_scopes` map and allocates owned String keys for every scored app

result.coverage_notes: All six slice files were read end to end: audit/mod.rs, credentials.rs, types.rs, permissions.rs, scoring.rs, scoring/tests.rs (the full 2123 lines). docs/architecture/audit-findings-and-remediation.md read fully. Supporting reads were partial and targeted: crates/azapptoolkit-core/src/scoping.rs lines 1-520 (the predicates the scorer calls; the tests and the ~600 lines after were not read), apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/commands/audit.rs only around the two scorer call sites (1225-1300, 1470-1625) and the CSV header, commands/remediation.rs handler signatures + the remove-expired body, web-rs audit_view/filter.rs (1-140), groups.rs (36-140, 236-320), row.rs via grep only, permission_picker.rs (236-335, 436-456), dialogs/scope_remediation.rs (40-125). No cargo build/test/clippy was run, so numeric claims (e.g. score deltas) are derived from reading the constants, not from executing the tests. The legacy PowerShell module the citations refer to is not in the repo, so rule-vs-legacy parity could not be checked beyond internal consistency.

result.area_summary: The auth slice is in good shape where it has clearly been burned before: keyring chunking with a count marker and fail-closed load, meticulous AADSTS redaction in logs, PKCE + CSRF state + OIDC nonce binding, tid/oid re-binding after every interactive flow, and a launch restore that refuses a remembered account from another tenant. Weak spots are consistency rather than intent: the documented "CAE-ness must match the adapter" rule is broken by every interactive flow (sign_in, consent, reauth, refresh, restore) because CAE-ness is not in the cache key; `interaction_required`/`login_required` are treated as a dead refresh token and purge the whole session; sign-out tears down the in-memory session before the fallible keyring delete so a failure leaves a half-signed-out state the next launch revives; and a domain-form tenant id that the config screen explicitly accepts can never pass `sign_in`'s tid check. The interactive flow is untestable end to end (hard-wired browser open), the token endpoint has no retry, and several docs/comments still describe the pre-`TokenError` "BearerProvider flattens to String" world.

findings.title: Domain-form tenant id is accepted by the config screen but can never sign in (tid check compares a GUID to the domain)
findings.rationale: `AppState::new` passes the configured tenant string straight into `EntraAuthService::new` (state.rs:258) and nothing resolves a domain to its GUID (grep: no openid-configuration lookup outside `commands/sso`). The `tid` claim is always the tenant GUID, so with `tenant_id = "contoso.onmicrosoft.com"` (which `set_auth_config` validates and saves, message: "Directory (tenant) ID must be a GUID or a tenant domain") the exchange succeeds at Entra and then fails locally with `token_exchange`, whose sign-in hint tells the operator to "verify the app's client and tenant IDs". `UserSettings::remembered_account_for(&self.tenant_id)` (settings.rs:162-165) compares the GUID from the claims to the domain too, so even if sign-in were relaxed, launch restore would be refused every time. A configuration path the UI advertises is unusable end to end.
findings.proposal: Resolve a non-GUID tenant once to its GUID and use that as the effective `tenant_id`: either at `AppState::new` via `{auth_root}/{tenant}/v2.0/.well-known/openid-configuration` (the repo already does this discovery in `commands/sso/mod.rs:101`; the `issuer` carries the GUID), or lazily in `sign_in` (accept when `self.tenant_id` is not a GUID, then store the resolved GUID for `remembered_account_for` and the keyring key). Add a `sign_in`-level test with a mock `/token` returning a GUID `tid` against a domain-configured service (needs finding on browser-opener injection), and a `settings.rs` test that a domain-configured tenant restores. Alternatively drop domain support from `is_valid_tenant` and say so in the first-run UI; today the two disagree.

findings.title: sign_out tears down the in-memory session before the fallible keyring delete; on failure the restore pointer and data caches survive and the UI message is wrong
findings.rationale: If `delete_refresh_token` errors (locked Secret Service, Credential Manager hiccup, `ensure_keyring_store` failure), `sign_out` returns `Err` after `known_tenants` and the token cache were already cleared, and the command returns before `forget_account()` and `state.cache.invalidate_tenant(...)`. Result: (a) every subsequent command fails `not_signed_in` while the shell stays mounted and the toast says "you are still signed in" — false; (b) `settings.json.last_account` and the keyring refresh token both survive, so the NEXT launch `restore_session` revives the exact session the operator just tried to end — the fail-open direction on a shared workstation; (c) the tenant's data caches (`state.cache`) are not swept, contradicting the comment that sign-out "must" drop every tenant-scoped entry. The doc on `forget_account` says the two must not disagree about whether anyone is signed in; this path makes them disagree.
findings.proposal: Make sign-out fail-safe: in `EntraAuthService::sign_out` attempt `delete_refresh_token` FIRST (via `spawn_blocking`, see the inline-keyring finding) and only then clear `cache`/`known_tenants`; in the command, run `forget_account()`, client removal and `state.cache.invalidate_tenant` unconditionally (before or regardless of the keyring result) and return the keyring error afterwards so the toast can say precisely "signed out, but the OS credential store still holds a token — remove the azapptoolkit entry manually". Update the shell.rs message accordingly. Add a service test with a keyring store that fails `delete_credential` (a small `keyring_core::CredentialStoreApi` fake) asserting `known_tenants` is empty AND the error is returned.

findings.title: CAE-ness is not part of the token cache key, and every interactive/restore flow seeds the Graph slots with non-CAE tokens — violating the invariant state.rs documents
findings.rationale: `graph_for` (state.rs:417-464) builds every Graph adapter with `ScopedTokenAdapter::new_cae`, i.e. it expects `cp1`-advertised tokens in the `(tenant, scope_key)` slot. But `sign_in` (mod.rs:332), `consent_for_scopes` (381-388), `reauthenticate` (661-669), `refresh_session` (583) and `restore_session` (617) all put a token minted WITHOUT the `claims` parameter into those same slots. `authorize_url` (114-152) also sends no `claims`. So after launch (restore), after "Refresh Token", after every "Grant consent", and after reauth the Graph read/write adapters serve a non-CAE token for up to its full lifetime — exactly the class of bug the state.rs comment forbids for the `ensure_*` probes and that `readiness.rs:272-291` goes out of its way to avoid. CAE tokens are the ones that revoke promptly on password reset / disabled user / risky sign-in, which is the security property the app opted into.
findings.proposal: Make it structural: include CAE-ness in the cache key (`TokenCache::get/put` take a `cae: bool` folded into `scope_key`, or a `CacheSlot { scopes, cae }`), so a non-CAE seed can never be served to a `new_cae` adapter — the worst case becomes one extra silent refresh. Then have the five flows mint CAE for Graph audiences: pass `claims = build_cae_claims(None)` on the `/authorize` and `/token` requests in `run_auth_code_flow` when the scope set is a Graph one, and use `access_token_for_scopes_cae(.., None)` in `refresh_session`/`restore_session`. Add a wiremock test asserting the `claims` form field is present on the refresh for a Graph scope set and that `cache.get(tenant, read_scopes, cae=true)` is what `graph_for` consumes.

findings.title: `interaction_required` / `login_required` are classified as a dead refresh token and purge the whole session; MSAL treats them as a per-resource step-up with the RT still valid
findings.rationale: AADSTS50076/50079/50158 (MFA / registration / external challenge required by Conditional Access for THIS resource) come back from a `refresh_token` grant as `error: "interaction_required"`; AADSTS50074 similarly. The refresh token remains fully valid for other audiences — MSAL surfaces `InteractionRequiredAuthError` and re-acquires interactively for that resource without discarding the account. Here a first ARM/Exchange/Log Analytics call under a "Require MFA for Azure management" or authentication-strength policy deletes the keyring token, drops every cached access token and forgets the tenant, so Graph browsing dies too and the operator gets the `Re-authenticate` (`prompt=login`) toast. In the per-resource authentication-strength case the reauth mints only the Graph read token, the next ARM refresh fails again, and the purge repeats — a loop. The frontend's own hint table already treats these codes as "complete the MFA prompt", not "session dead", so the two layers disagree. error.rs:11-16 states the RT "must be discarded" for `interaction_required`; that premise is what this finding challenges.
findings.proposal: Add `AuthError::InteractionRequired(String)` (UI code `interaction_required`, not in `REAUTH_FATAL_CODES`, `retryable=false`) for `interaction_required`/`login_required` and for `invalid_grant` whose AADSTS is 50074/50076/50079/50158; do NOT purge in `access_token_inner` for it (mirror the `ConsentRequired` arm). Recover with a scope-targeted interactive round trip: generalise `consent_for_scopes` into `interactive_for_scopes(tenant, scopes, prompt)` and expose a `request_scope_step_up(tenant_id, feature)` command (or reuse `request_scope_consent` with `prompt=login`), and teach `Session::report_command_error` to offer "Verify identity" on that code. Pin with wiremock tests: `interaction_required` keeps the keyring token and `known_tenants`; 70008 still purges.

findings.title: Loopback honours an `error=` redirect before validating `state`, and writes the success page before the state check
findings.rationale: RFC 6749 §4.1.2.1 requires the error redirect to echo `state`, but the listener returns `Authorization(err)` on any request carrying `error=` without checking it. Any local process, or any web page open in the operator's browser (a cross-origin `fetch("http://127.0.0.1:<port>/?error=...")` still reaches the socket even though the response is opaque), can abort an in-flight sign-in and place an attacker-chosen string into the sign-in card (`"Sign-in failed: authorization request failed: {err}"`). The port is ephemeral but the range is small enough to spray. Separately, the browser tab is told "sign-in complete" even when `state` mismatches and the app is about to report `state_mismatch` — the page and the app disagree. `error_description` is also dropped, so the AADSTS code (65004 user-declined vs 53003 CA block) never reaches `aadsts_hint`.
findings.proposal: Reorder: parse `state` first; if it is absent or mismatched, respond 400 with a neutral page and `continue` the accept loop (a forged request should not end the wait) rather than returning; only after `state` matches branch on `error`/`code`. Whitelist the surfaced `error` value (known OAuth codes) and carry `extract_aadsts_code(error_description)` into the message via `redacted_aad_error`-style formatting so the existing hint table fires. Extend `state_mismatch_is_rejected` to assert the forged request does not terminate the listener and that a later valid redirect still succeeds.

findings.title: `consent_required` is flattened to `token_error` inside every client call, so the shared UI consent fallback never fires for scoped calls; docs still blame a `String` boundary that no longer exists
findings.rationale: `token_adapter::token_error` (token_adapter.rs:21-29) now carries `consent_required` across the boundary as `TokenError { code: "consent_required", .. }`, but `ui_code()` only passes the two re-auth-fatal codes through and collapses everything else to `token_error`. So a Graph write/sharepoint/policy call that hits a missing consent still reaches the UI as `token_error`, and `Session::report_consent_required` (web-rs/state/errors.rs:112-117, keyed on `e.code == "consent_required"`) — described in the doc as "one shared fallback" for commands with no bespoke button — cannot fire. The `ensure_*` pre-acquisitions remain necessary only because of this second flattening, yet the doc, `.claude/rules/auth.md:18` and five `state.rs` comments (558, 617, 627, 655, …) attribute it to a `String` boundary that was removed. `consent_required` is already asserted non-fatal (reauth.rs:263) and non-retryable, so passing it through is safe for fan-outs (bulk.rs:1190-1197 treats it as per-item).
findings.proposal: Introduce `core::reauth::PASSTHROUGH_CODES = REAUTH_FATAL_CODES ∪ {"consent_required"}` (or make `passthrough_code` return `Some` for any non-empty classified `TokenError.code` and let `is_reauth_fatal` stay separate) so `GraphError/ArmError/ExchangeError/KeyVaultError::ui_code()` emit `consent_required`. Then rewrite the doc paragraph, `.claude/rules/auth.md`, and the `state.rs` comments to the true statement: the `ensure_*` probes exist to surface consent BEFORE side-effecting work and to bind a specific `consent_feature`, not because the boundary loses the code. Add a dto test: `UiError::from(GraphError::Token(TokenError::new("consent_required", ..))).code == "consent_required"`.

findings.title: Token endpoint calls have no retry/backoff; the readiness probe fans out six refreshes at once and a 429/5xx surfaces as a terminal `token_exchange`
findings.rationale: AGENTS.md makes `core::http_retry` the one retry budget ("incl. `$batch`"), and every REST client honours `Retry-After`, but the `/token` POST is a single attempt: a 429 from `login.microsoftonline.com` (which does throttle per client/tenant and returns `Retry-After`) or a transient 5xx/network error becomes `TokenExchange("HTTP 429")` → UI `token_exchange` (retryable=true but nothing retries), readiness shows `Unknown` for that half, and a `ScopedTokenAdapter::bearer()` failure aborts the Graph request that needed it. The readiness checklist and the per-audience refresh locks (token_cache.rs:226-229: "Access Readiness fans about six out at once") make simultaneous token requests the normal case, not an edge.
findings.proposal: Wrap the send in `azapptoolkit_core::http_retry::with_retries("aad_token", RetryClass::<idempotent>, |_| async { .. })`, classifying 429 (`Retry-After`), 5xx and `reqwest` transport errors as `Attempt::Retry` and everything else as `Done`. A `refresh_token` grant is idempotent (Entra does not revoke on use), so retrying is safe; an `authorization_code` exchange is single-use, so restrict retries there to transport errors before a response was received. Add a wiremock test: first 429 with `Retry-After: 1`, then 200 → token cached, exactly two requests.

findings.title: Sign-in hard-fails after a successful browser round trip when no OS keyring is available (headless/minimal Linux); no in-memory fallback
findings.rationale: On Linux the only store is the D-Bus Secret Service; on a box without a session bus or `gnome-keyring`/`kwallet` (SSH + X forwarding, WSLg, minimal WMs, some containers) `Store::new()` fails, `ensure_keyring_store` memoises the failure forever (token_cache.rs:26-42), and `store_token_outcome` discards a perfectly good access token and returns `Keyring` — AFTER the operator completed the browser sign-in. The hint ("unlock ... then retry") cannot be followed because there is nothing to unlock, and every retry repeats the browser round trip. Nothing in README/DEVELOPMENT documents Secret Service as a hard requirement (README:326 still says "libsecret").
findings.proposal: Add a process-local fallback: when `ensure_keyring_store` fails, keep the refresh token in a `Zeroizing<String>` inside `EntraAuthService` (an `enum RefreshStore { Keyring, Memory(Mutex<HashMap<(tenant,oid), Zeroizing<String>>>) }` selected once), return `Ok` from `store_token_outcome`, and surface a one-time `keyring_unavailable` notice so the UI can say "signed in for this session only; the session won't survive a restart". `restore_session` naturally returns `Ok(None)` next launch. Document the Linux requirement (and `AZAPPTOOLKIT_...` override if any) in README/DEVELOPMENT. Test: a `keyring_core` store whose `new` fails → sign-in-shaped flow still yields a cached access token.

findings.title: `AuthError::Cancelled` is never constructed; the two real cancel paths (300 s timeout, `access_denied`) surface as `loopback`/`authorization` with misleading hints
findings.rationale: grep shows `AuthError::Cancelled` appears only in error.rs and the dto mapping — dead on the backend — while the frontend keeps a hint for the `cancelled` code that can never be reached. Meanwhile the two ways an operator actually cancels (closing the tab → 300 s later `Loopback("timed out…")` → code `loopback` → "Check your network and try again"; clicking Cancel on the consent screen → `error=access_denied` → `Authorization("access_denied")` → "The sign-in was declined. An administrator may need to grant the app consent") both produce the wrong advice. `dispatch`/DR already use a `cancelled` code meaningfully (dr.rs:81), so the vocabulary exists.
findings.proposal: Map the loopback timeout to `AuthError::Cancelled` (or a dedicated `Timeout` with its own code and hint), and map an `error=access_denied` redirect whose `error_description` carries no AADSTS code to `Cancelled` as well; keep `Authorization` for everything else and carry the AADSTS code through (see the loopback finding). Update the `From<AuthError> for UiError` test table (already lists `Cancelled`) and add a loopback test for the `error=` arm. Remove the variant instead if the team prefers the current codes — but then delete the frontend hint too.

findings.title: Browser launch failure is only logged; the authorize URL is never surfaced, so the operator waits out the full 300 s with no way to proceed
findings.rationale: The warning says "user must open URL manually", but the full URL (with `state`, `code_challenge`) is — correctly — not logged anywhere and is not returned to the UI, so there is nothing for the user to open. On a desktop with no default browser handler, a snap/flatpak-confined `xdg-open`, or a Windows policy that blocks the handler, sign-in silently hangs until the 300 s timeout and then shows a network hint. grep of web-rs finds no "copy link"/manual-open affordance.
findings.proposal: Emit the authorize URL to the webview when the launcher fails: have `run_auth_code_flow` take an `on_open_failed: impl Fn(&Url)` callback (or return `AuthError::BrowserLaunch(url)` early while keeping the listener alive in a spawned task), and in `commands::auth::sign_in` forward it via a Tauri event so the sign-in card can render a "Couldn't open your browser — copy this link" button. The URL is single-use and bound by PKCE/state, so exposing it to the operator's own webview is safe. Also lowers the timeout's cost by giving a visible next step.

findings.title: No test proves the single-flight refresh: N concurrent requests for one scope set should produce exactly one /token POST
findings.rationale: The struct doc (mod.rs:71-76) promises "same-key concurrency still collapses to one network call via the double-checked cache read taken under the lock", and the token_cache doc leans on it for keyring write safety, but the only test (`refresh_locks_are_keyed_per_tenant_and_scope_set`, 749-761) checks lock identity, not behaviour. A future edit that moves the second cache check, or makes `bypass_cache` sticky, would silently turn every Graph page walk into a refresh storm (each `bearer()` call hits this path) and multiply keyring writes — the exact splice hazard the chunk lock was added for.
findings.proposal: Add `#[tokio::test] concurrent_same_scope_requests_collapse_to_one_token_call`: mount the success mock with `.expect(1)`, seed `signed_in_service`, `join_all` eight `access_token_for_scopes` futures for the same scopes, assert all eight return the same token string and `server.verify()` passes; add a sibling asserting two DIFFERENT scope sets produce two POSTs (proves the per-key locks do not serialise unrelated audiences). Also cover `access_token_for_scopes_cae(.., Some(challenge))` bypassing the cache and sending a `claims` form field (wiremock `body_string_contains("claims=")`).

findings.title: The interactive flow is untestable (hard-wired browser launch + internal listener), so sign_in's tid check, the nonce check, consent identity rejection and reauthenticate have no end-to-end test
findings.rationale: Because `open_system_browser` is called unconditionally and the redirect port is private to the function, no test can drive `sign_in`, `consent_for_scopes` or `reauthenticate`: the test module covers `ensure_same_identity` in isolation (1027-1061), `authorize_url` shape, and the silent paths only. Untested security-relevant branches: `id_token nonce mismatch` (294-296), `id token tid … does not match configured tenant` (313-318), `id token missing tid/oid` (306-321), the `consent`/`re-authentication` mismatch wiring (376, 660), `store_token_outcome` with `scope_fallback = &[]` at sign-in, and that `reauthenticate` re-inserts `known_tenants` only after validation. The wiremock harness already exists; only the seam is missing.
findings.proposal: Inject the launcher: add a `browser: Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> Result<()> + Send + Sync>` (default `open_system_browser`) to `EntraAuthService` with a `with_browser_opener` constructor for tests. A test opener parses the URL, extracts `redirect_uri`/`state`/`nonce`, and spawns a task that connects to the loopback port with `GET /?code=…&state=…`; the wiremock `/token` returns an id_token built with `URL_SAFE_NO_PAD` carrying the chosen `tid`/`oid`/`nonce`. Then add tests for: happy sign-in caches under read scopes; wrong `tid` rejected; nonce mismatch rejected; consent completed as a different `oid` rejected and cache untouched; reauth restores `known_tenants`. This also unlocks the domain-tenant and CAE fixes' tests.

findings.title: Zeroize discipline is one-sided: the load path is meticulous, but the freshly issued refresh token, the raw /token body and the PKCE verifier are dropped un-wiped
findings.rationale: `load_refresh_token` (token_cache.rs:303-373) documents at length why every chunk is wiped and returns `Zeroizing<String>`, `AccessToken` zeroizes on drop, and `Debug` redacts — but on every refresh the NEW refresh token (`TokenResponse.refresh_token: Option<String>`) is dropped as a plain `String` at the end of the `spawn_blocking` closure, the entire response body containing all three tokens sits in `bytes` and is freed un-wiped, and `serde_json` builds intermediate `String`s for each field. `oauth2-5.0.0/src/types.rs` has no `zeroize`, so the `Zeroizing` copy of the verifier leaves the original in place. Either the heap-wipe property matters (then these leaks defeat it on every refresh) or it does not (then the load-path ceremony is misleading). DEVELOPMENT.md:342-345 presents zeroize-on-drop as an invariant reviewers check.
findings.proposal: Make `TokenResponse.refresh_token`/`access_token`/`id_token` `Zeroizing<String>` (serde supports `Zeroizing<T>` via `#[serde(deserialize_with)]` or a small newtype), wrap `bytes` in `Zeroizing<Vec<u8>>` (`bytes.to_vec()` then zeroize; or read into a `Zeroizing<Vec<u8>>` via `chunk()`), and drop the theatre around the PKCE verifier (either generate the verifier locally with `Zeroizing` + `Sha256` or accept the copy and remove the misleading wrapper). Small, mechanical; add a doc line in DEVELOPMENT.md listing exactly which buffers are wiped so the claim matches the code.

findings.title: Two keyring deletes run inline on the tokio runtime (sign_out and the InvalidGrant purge) and take the std `CHUNK_SET_LOCK` on a worker thread, contrary to the documented spawn_blocking rule
findings.rationale: Save and load were moved to `spawn_blocking` precisely because Credential Manager / Secret Service calls block and the chunk loop makes N of them (plus one probe). `delete_chunks` does the same loop, and `delete_refresh_token` blocks on `CHUNK_SET_LOCK` — a std mutex that a `spawn_blocking` writer may be holding for the duration of its own keyring round trips. Doing that from `access_token_inner` (which also holds the per-scope async refresh lock) or `sign_out` parks a tokio worker for the whole time; on Linux the first call may also block on D-Bus connection setup inside `ensure_keyring_store`. Not a correctness bug today, but it is the pattern the crate's own comments say not to write.
findings.proposal: Add `async fn delete_refresh_token_blocking(tenant, oid)` (or reuse the `spawn_blocking` shape in `store_token_outcome`) and use it at both sites; in the purge arm, `spawn_blocking` and ignore the join result as today. Consider a `repo_invariants` source-scan test that every `save_/load_/delete_refresh_token(` call outside `token_cache.rs` sits inside `spawn_blocking`.

findings.title: Dead code in the auth surface: `tenants()` is an async fn with no await and no callers; `EXCHANGE_SCOPES` is unused and hardcodes the commercial host while the scope catalog re-derives it
findings.rationale: `grep -rn "\.tenants()"` across `apps/` and `crates/` returns nothing; the frontend binding header (`bindings/auth.rs:1`) still advertises a `current_tenants` command that `generate_handler!` (lib.rs:45-50) does not register. `EXCHANGE_SCOPES` is referenced only from doc comments: `default_exchange_scopes` builds the cloud-correct value itself, so the constant is both dead and wrong for sovereign clouds, and the doc comment claims a derivation that does not happen. Both are small, but the auth crate is the one place the repo says to read before editing, so stale surface here costs reviewer attention.
findings.proposal: Delete `tenants()` (or make it sync and use it in `prove_tenant_session`-style diagnostics if wanted) and fix the `bindings/auth.rs` module doc. Change `EXCHANGE_SCOPES` to the bare permission (`&["Exchange.Manage"]`) and have `default_exchange_scopes` map it through `exchange_resource()` like `graph_scopes` does — or remove the constant and the two comments that cite it. Zero behaviour change.

findings.title: Docs describe pre-refactor auth plumbing: 'extend BOTH matches! sets', `service.rs::…` paths, hwchen `keyring`/libsecret, and a broken `[`keyring`]` intra-doc link
findings.rationale: `core::reauth::REAUTH_FATAL_CODES` is now the single definition (reauth.rs:208 "Adding a code is one edit: this slice"), so the doc's instruction to edit two `matches!` sets sends a contributor hunting for code that no longer exists and contradicts AGENTS.md. `service.rs` was split into `service/{mod,wire,loopback,scopes}.rs`; three docs still cite the old path (`classify_token_error`/`redacted_aad_error` live in `service/wire.rs`). The keyring is `keyring-core` + `zbus-secret-service-keyring-store` (pure-Rust Secret Service, not libsecret) per Cargo.toml:21,43-45; README still credits hwchen `keyring`, and the `[`keyring`]` rustdoc links in lib.rs:5 and token_cache.rs:6-7 resolve to nothing (`cargo doc` warns).
findings.proposal: Update auth-and-consent.md:118 to "add the code to `core::reauth::REAUTH_FATAL_CODES`; both predicates derive from it"; replace the three `service.rs::` citations with `service/wire.rs::` / `service/mod.rs`; README: "Secret Service (via zbus)" and `keyring-core`; change the rustdoc links to plain `keyring-core` text or `[`keyring_core`]`. Consider a `repo_invariants/sources.rs`-style test that every `crates/.../src/<file>.rs::` path cited in `docs/**/*.md` exists.

findings.title: InvalidGrant purge deletes whatever refresh token is in the keyring, not the one it used — a late-failing refresh can erase a freshly re-authenticated token
findings.rationale: Refresh locks are per `(tenant, scope_key)` by design, so two audiences refresh concurrently with the same RT. If refresh A (say ARM, on a slow link) is in flight when the session is re-established — `reauthenticate` or `consent_for_scopes` stores RT2 and re-inserts `known_tenants` — and A then returns `invalid_grant` for RT1, the arm deletes RT2 and removes the tenant: the operator who just completed a browser round trip is immediately "signed out" again and the reauth toast reappears. The window is a few seconds around every reauth, and the readiness fan-out (six concurrent refreshes) plus a 30 s HTTP timeout make it reachable. The purge should be conditional on the keyring still holding the token that failed.
findings.proposal: Keep a monotonically increasing `session_generation: AtomicU64` bumped by `store_token_outcome`; capture it before `post_token` in `access_token_inner` and skip the purge (return `RefreshTokenMissing` without deleting/removing) when the generation changed — or compare the loaded RT to the stored one under `CHUNK_SET_LOCK` before deleting (`delete_refresh_token_if_eq`). Test: with a wiremock delay on one scope set, complete a `reauthenticate`-shaped store during the delay, then assert the keyring still holds RT2 and `known_tenants` is intact after the delayed `invalid_grant`.

findings.title: `token_adapter::token_error` duplicates the `From<AuthError> for UiError` code table by hand with a 'must match' comment but no test pinning agreement
findings.rationale: `grep -rn "token_error(" apps/desktop/src-tauri` finds only the definition — no test exercises it. AGENTS.md calls this function "the sole mapping" at the `BearerProvider` boundary and the repo has invested a whole module (`core::reauth`) in preventing exactly this kind of two-table drift for the fatal codes; the third code (`consent_required`) and any future one are still a hand-copied pair. A variant renamed or added on the dto side (e.g. the `InteractionRequired` proposal) would compile here and silently fall to `token_error`.
findings.proposal: Either derive: `TokenError::new(UiError::from(err).code, ..)` if the dependency direction allows (src-tauri already depends on dto), collapsing the duplicate; or add a unit test in `token_adapter.rs` iterating the same constructible `AuthError` cases as `auth_error_maps_to_stable_code_and_retryable` and asserting `token_error(e).code == UiError::from(e).code` for the classified variants and `"token_error"` for the rest.

crates/azapptoolkit-auth/src/error.rs:14 — doc says `interaction_required` means "the refresh token is no longer usable"; see the interaction_required finding — the doc encodes the wrong premise.

result.area_summary: The core-infra-b slice is in good shape where it has been fought over: the scoping gates (resource-aware Exchange/SharePoint predicates, Selected-scope levels, `selected_scope_accepts`) are exhaustively tested and match Microsoft's model, the federation and redirect validators close real userinfo-host tricks, and every Entra/Azure role GUID in the capabilities catalog and azure_roles is correct. The weak spots are places where Microsoft moved after the code was written: the FIC model cannot deserialize a flexible federated credential (null `subject`), the mailbox advisory's name-shaped fallback misses the `MailboxItem.*` / `MailboxFolder.*` / `Mail-Advanced.*` application permissions that Exchange RBAC now scopes, the restore's identifier-URI rewrite handles only one of Microsoft's two "default" URI forms, and the sovereign-cloud selector is runtime-env only while the client/tenant ids are bakeable. A handful of consistency items (seven `Vec` fields without the file's own `null_to_default` rule, commercial-host scope strings in the catalog, a CSP allowlist the webview never uses, duplicated GUID literals) round it out.

Because `Paged<FederatedIdentityCredential>` is deserialized as one document, a single flexible FIC on an app makes `list_federated_credentials` fail with `invalid type: null, expected a string`, so the Federated credentials tab errors for that app and, worse, the DR backup records the whole application as skipped. No test covers a null subject, and `claimsMatchingExpression` appears nowhere in the repo.

Propagate: `FederatedCredentialDto.subject: Option<String>` (render 'expression: …' when subject is None), `validate_federated_credential` takes `subject: Option<&str>` plus `expression: Option<&str>` and requires exactly one, `fic_dto`/restore either recreate a flexible FIC through the beta endpoint or emit a 'was NOT restored — flexible credential' warning instead of skipping the app. Expected effect: apps with flexible FICs list, back up and restore instead of disappearing.

findings.title: Mailbox advisory's name-shaped fallback misses MailboxItem.*/MailboxFolder.*/Mail-Advanced.* — org-wide read/write of every mailbox item scores as all-clear
findings.rationale: `starts_with("MailboxSettings.")` does not match `MailboxItem.*`/`MailboxFolder.*`, and `starts_with("Mail.")` does not match `Mail-Advanced.*`, so the fallback fails exactly the case its own comment says it exists for. A Microsoft Graph application grant of `MailboxItem.ReadWrite.All` or `Mail-Advanced.ReadWrite.All` (tenant-wide read/write of all mailbox content) enters neither the mailbox advisory nor the high-risk list: no finding, no ScopeMailboxAccess fix, healthy-looking score. docs/architecture/exchange-scoping.md:46-49 deliberately keeps these out of `graph_mail_role` (scopability/AAP parity), but that decision is about the *fix* gate, not advisory membership — `is_mailbox_reaching_permission` is documented as a superset ("over-reporting is the safe side", scoping.rs:210).
findings.proposal: (1) Extend `mailbox_named` with `"MailboxFolder."`, `"MailboxItem."`, `"Mail-Advanced."` (and `"MailboxConfigItem."`) and add a table test asserting `is_mailbox_reaching_permission(Some(GRAPH), v)` for every value in Microsoft's supported-roles table. (2) Add `Mail-Advanced.ReadWrite.All`, `MailboxItem.ReadWrite.All`, `MailboxItem.ImportExport.All`, `MailboxItem.Export.All`, `MailboxFolder.ReadWrite.All` to HIGH_RISK_APP_PERMISSIONS and the read variants to MEDIUM (the existing 'broader side must be scored' test convention). (3) Optionally, since all six ARE RBAC-scopable, add them to `graph_mail_role` with the CHANGELOG note exchange-scoping.md requires. Effect: these grants produce a mailbox finding (unconfinable-org-wide today, scopable after step 3) instead of silence.

findings.title: rewrite_identifier_uris only rewrites the exact `api://{appId}` form; `api://{tenantId}/{appId}`, `api://{string}/{appId}` and `api://{tenantId}/...` fail the Expose-an-API PATCH on restore
findings.rationale: `api://{tenantId}/{appId}` is one of Microsoft's two 'default' identifier URIs (the only two allowed once an org enables `nonDefaultUriAddition`), and `api://{string}/{appId}` is a common alternative. Both keep the SOURCE appId (and, cross-tenant, the SOURCE tenant GUID), which the destination tenant rejects because the GUID matches neither the new appId nor the destination tenant. The failure is not isolated: the identifier URIs share one PATCH with `oauth2PermissionScopes` and `preAuthorizedApplications`, so the app's whole Expose-an-API surface is lost with a single warning line. The backup carries `source_tenant_id` and the restore knows the destination tenant, so a correct rewrite is possible.
findings.proposal: Change the helper to `rewrite_identifier_uris(uris, source_app_id, new_app_id, source_tenant_id, dest_tenant_id)` and rewrite every `api://` URI whose host or path segment equals `source_app_id` → `new_app_id` or equals `source_tenant_id` → `dest_tenant_id` (segment-wise, case-insensitive GUID compare; leave `https://` and verified-domain forms untouched). Add table tests for `api://{tenant}/{app}`, `api://{tenant}/api`, `api://productapi/{app}`, and a substring non-match. Update docs/architecture/backup-and-restore.md:148 ("`api://{old}` → `api://{new}`"). Effect: cross-tenant restores keep their Expose-an-API configuration instead of dropping URIs, scopes and pre-authorized clients together.

findings.title: AZAPPTOOLKIT_CLOUD is runtime-env only; a baked sovereign-cloud installer is impossible even though client/tenant ids are baked
findings.rationale: The whole point of build-time baking (README, build.rs doc comment) is that a team distributes one installer and recipients configure nothing. A GCC High / DoD / 21Vianet team cannot get that today: the cloud is read only from the process environment at runtime, so every recipient must set `AZAPPTOOLKIT_CLOUD` or the app silently targets the commercial endpoints and sign-in fails with an unhelpful AADSTS error. The settings screen also has no cloud field (README resolution order covers only client/tenant ids).
findings.proposal: In build.rs add `"AZAPPTOOLKIT_CLOUD" => "AZAPPTOOLKIT_BUILD_CLOUD"` (plus a `rerun-if-env-changed`), and in `CloudEnvironment::from_env` fall back to `option_env!("AZAPPTOOLKIT_BUILD_CLOUD")` (or have the auth service read the baked value the same way state.rs does for the ids) before defaulting to Commercial. Document in README/DEVELOPMENT.md that `.env` may carry `AZAPPTOOLKIT_CLOUD`. Effect: one `.env` line produces a sovereign-cloud installer that needs no per-workstation env var.

findings.title: Seven Vec fields use bare #[serde(default)] without null_to_default, contradicting the file's own null-tolerance rule
findings.evidence:
models.rs:13-17 (the rule):
